requirements.requirement: Implement the log-forwarding setup using Ansible run against node1/node2
requirements.summary: An Ansible inventory and 3-play playbook were authored on the control node (node3) and executed via ansible-playbook, with a preceding successful ansible ping to both hosts and a full run reporting ok/changed with zero failures across both nodes.

requirements.requirement: Forward the inventory application's log messages from node2 to a centralized collector on node1
requirements.summary: node1 was configured with imudp/imtcp listeners on port 514 (confirmed listening on 0.0.0.0:514/[::]:514), and a logger-generated message tagged 'inventory' on node2 was observed arriving and being written on node1, demonstrating live end-to-end forwarding. No real 'inventory' service exists in this environment (confirmed by discovery), so the executor reasonably used the programname/tag 'inventory' as the log source identifier, which is a defensible interpretation given the environment's contents.

requirements.requirement: Persist received messages on node1 under /var/log/inventory/node2.log
requirements.summary: After the playbook run, /var/log/inventory/ was created on node1 and a logger test message from node2 appeared verbatim in /var/log/inventory/node2.log; subsequent test messages continued to append to the same file across the session.

requirements.requirement: Log flow keeps working after node2 restarts
requirements.summary: Healthy baseline (boot-id c0691b74..., rsyslog active/enabled) was captured, a reboot was triggered and directly observed as a connection timeout (disruption), a new boot-id (bde232b6...) confirmed the restart, rsyslog was again active/enabled post-boot, and a freshly logged message from node2 was confirmed appended to node1's node2.log — showing the complete baseline/disruption/recovery transition.

requirements.requirement: Log flow keeps working after node1 restarts
requirements.summary: Healthy baseline (boot-id 29011044..., rsyslog active/enabled) was captured, a reboot was triggered and observed as a connection timeout, a new boot-id (0bcb3c7a...) confirmed the restart, rsyslog was active/enabled and listening on 514 again, the log directory/file were intact, and a new message logged from node2 was confirmed to arrive in the file — demonstrating full recovery of the pipeline after node1's restart.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task were satisfied: an Ansible playbook run from the control node configured rsyslog-based centralized forwarding of 'inventory'-tagged messages from node2 to node1, persisted them at /var/log/inventory/node2.log, and the pipeline was directly verified to survive and recover from restarts of both node1 and node2 (baseline boot-id, disruption via connection timeout, new boot-id, and confirmed log delivery post-restart for each). The provider-wide restart protocol was also applied to node3 and all boot-identity transitions are corroborated by the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Hygiene is good overall, with only a minor, low-risk residue of unused base64 intermediate files left on the control node.
limitations: No real 'inventory' application exists in this environment; the executor used logger with tag 'inventory' as a stand-in for the application's log source, which is a reasonable but assumed interpretation given the task's premise.

ssh.service was observed disabled/inactive on node1 after its restart; this reflects pre-existing baseline configuration rather than an executor regression, but it means SSH-based re-administration of node1 would not work without another restart or manual intervention (not required by the task).

operational_hygiene.summary: State-changing commands were largely necessary prerequisites: regenerating missing SSH host keys and restarting ssh on node1/node2 (cmd-72b33595e8bf48a3, cmd-622c8ad58ef74a48) were required after discovering ssh.service had failed due to missing host keys, and setting up passwordless SSH (cmd-846218ca8ef34599, cmd-4d28d8fd1dfb4d97, cmd-440e69a468eb4df6) was needed for Ansible connectivity from the control node. One minor residue item: base64-encoded intermediate copies of the playbook and templates were written to /root/log-collector on the control node (cmd-0dca97ead8a74f14, cmd-5479a7179fdf4cbd) and never removed after being decoded into the final files; this is low-risk, bounded to the control node, and does not affect managed-node state, but it is unnecessary leftover residue. After-executor snapshots show no failed services and no other unexplained package or exposure changes on any of the three nodes; the new port-514 listeners on node1 and restored ssh listener on node2 are expected, task-required exposure. ssh.service remained disabled (not enabled at boot) on node1/node2 after restart, but this was pre-existing baseline state (unit was already 'disabled; preset: enabled' before the executor touched it) and not a regression the executor introduced.
